hypothesis: If the claim holds, the haploid (germ-nucleus) chromosome number n is between 6 and 16 for a large majority of species, with fewer species below 6 than in 6–16, and fewer species above 16 than below 6.
pass_criterion: Across species with a recorded haploid number n, at least 80% have 6 <= n <= 16, the fraction with n < 6 is under 10%, and the fraction with n > 16 is under the fraction with n < 6. All three conditions must hold. The fractions are computed on one modal n per species.
fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if fewer than 70% of species have 6 <= n <= 16. It is also refuted if the fraction with n > 16 is greater than or equal to the fraction with n < 6, which would contradict 'fewer still have more than sixteen'. Results between 70% and 80% in range count as inconclusive and are reported as not supporting the claim as stated.
interpretation: Thompson's 'chromosomes in the germ-nuclei' is the reduced (gametic) number, i.e. the haploid number n. For species where the database records only 2n, I take n = 2n/2. 'Few' and 'fewer still' are quantified as under 10% below 6 and a smaller fraction above 16. The unit is the species, using the modal reported count, so that well-studied species are not over-weighted. A modern reinterpretation is that polyploidy was unknown in 1917. Polyploid species are therefore kept in the main analysis, and a sensitivity analysis is run on diploid-level counts. The dataset covers vascular plants only, so this plan tests the plant part of the claim. The animal part would need a separate dataset, and no animal data enter this test. The conclusion is therefore limited to the plant half of 'plants and animals'.

dataset.name: Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB)
dataset.publisher: Tel Aviv University (Rice et al., Chromosome Counts Database project)
dataset.why_it_fits: CCDB compiles published chromosome counts per species and is downloadable and searchable. The fields used would be species name, gametophytic count (n) and sporophytic count (2n). I would take one modal n per species, with n = 2n/2 where only 2n is given, and then compute the share of species with n < 6, 6–16 and > 16. I have not independently verified the download format, and the database covers plants only.
